newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-Shoney's dissident seeks CEO post.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Shoney's dissident seeks CEO post.

text.p: Raymond Schoenbaum, son of the man who founded Shoney's restaurants, aims to be chairman and chief executive of the company if he is successful in his proxy fight to replace the company's board.
"I plan to turn the company around and make it successful," Schoenbaum, the son of founder Alex Schoenbaum, said in an interview. "We have taken a lot of wrong paths in the past few years."

Schoenbaum and his mother, who formed the Shoney's Shareholders Committee with their eight percent stake, filed to call for a special shareholder meeting to replace Shoney's board, amend its bylaws to keep only seven directors and repeal any amendments to the by-laws that have not been approved by shareholders since February 18, 1996.
Schoenbaum said food quality is the top problem at the chain, which posted $1.1 billion in sales for the year ended October 1996.
Shoney's chief administrative officer W. Craig Barber said he was "surprised" by Schoenbaum's plan to replace the board.
Barber noted that the Schoenbaum family has been represented on the board since the 1970s and Schoenbaum's brother has served on the board since 1996.
Shoney's board was re-elected three months ago with 80 percent of the vote, Barber said.

Schoenbaum, who has operated restaurant chains independently of Shoney's and taken a leave of absence from Applebee's International Inc's board, said he has offered his advice to improve the restaurant chain's operations, but Shoney's has not been receptive.
Schoenbaum said Shoney's share price has fallen sharply since 1993, while the number of customers coming into its restaurants has declined.
Barber declined to comment about the state of the company's share price, which closed at 6-1/2, up 1/8.
Schoenbaum said the move to replace the board is not meant to cast aspersions upon his brother, but to improve the chain which had a stock price as high as 25 in 1993.
Schoenbaum said he would not put the company up for sale if he won the proxy fight to replace the board and he is not planning to buy any more Shoney's stock.
"Shoney's is part of my family's legacy," he said.
